---
title: "M&M sampling"
format: html
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)     # For ggplot, dplyr, and friends
library(moderndive)    # For rep_slice_sample()
library(googlesheets4) # For reading the class Google Sheet

# Switch this to TRUE to use the class's data from the Google Sheet
use_class_data <- FALSE

sheet_url <- "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1s3E3GkKKRYntnAX5BbuFqhNUUYapItpcG9pYoUbB7-8/edit?usp=sharing"

# Change this to the name you typed in the form
my_name <- "Student 1"

# Google Forms makes column names from the question text, like "How many blue
# M&Ms do you have?". This finds the name column and the color word in each
# color column, and turns whatever students typed into numbers
clean_bags <- function(raw) {
  raw |>
    select(
      name = matches("name", ignore.case = TRUE),
      matches(
        "(^|[^a-z])(blue|brown|green|orange|red|yellow)([^a-z]|$)",
        ignore.case = TRUE
      )
    ) |>
    rename_with(
      \(x) str_extract(str_to_lower(x), "blue|brown|green|orange|red|yellow"),
      .cols = -name
    ) |>
    mutate(across(-name, \(x) parse_number(as.character(x)))) |>
    mutate(bag = row_number(), .before = 1)
}

# Simulated bags, drawn from a known color mix
sim_bags <- read_csv("data/mm_bags_simulated.csv")

if (use_class_data) {
  gs4_deauth()  # The sheet is public, so we don't need to log in
  bags <- read_sheet(sheet_url, col_types = "c") |> clean_bags()
} else {
  bags <- sim_bags
}

# The true color mix for the simulated bags (we never know this in real life!)
true_mix <- read_csv("data/mm_true_mix.csv")
true_p_green <- true_mix |> filter(color == "green") |> pull(p)

# Green M&Ms at the two US factories and on the old M&Ms website
reference_green <- tribble(
  ~source,                ~p_green,
  "Cleveland, TN",        0.198,
  "Hackettstown, NJ",     0.125,
  "2007 website numbers", 0.16
)

# A giant vat of 10,000 simulated M&Ms, one row per M&M
vat <- read_csv("data/mm_vat.csv")
```

## The data

Each row is one bag of M&Ms. The columns count how many of each color were in the bag.

```{r}
bags
```

We'll add the total number of M&Ms in each bag and each bag's proportion of green M&Ms ($\widehat{p}_\text{green}$):

```{r}
bags <- bags |>
  mutate(
    total = blue + brown + green + orange + red + yellow,
    p_hat_green = green / total
  )

bags |> select(bag, name, green, total, p_hat_green)
```

## Everyone's $\widehat{p}$ is different

Every bag is a sample, and every sample gives a slightly different estimate. This histogram is our class's sampling distribution:

```{r}
ggplot(bags, aes(x = p_hat_green)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.04, boundary = 0, color = "white", fill = "#31A84A") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of green M&Ms in each bag", y = "Number of bags")
```

## Pooling the whole class

Combining all the bags gives one giant sample:

```{r}
pooled_green <- bags |>
  summarize(
    bags = n(),
    green = sum(green),
    total = sum(total)
  ) |>
  mutate(p_hat = green / total)

pooled_green
```

How does our pooled estimate compare to the US factories and the old M&Ms website?

```{r}
reference_green |>
  add_row(source = "Our class", p_green = pooled_green$p_hat) |>
  mutate(source = fct_reorder(source, p_green)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p_green, y = source, fill = source == "Our class")) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(p_green)), hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "#31A84A"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Proportion of green M&Ms", y = NULL)
```

Whose bag was closest to the pooled estimate? Farthest?

```{r}
bags |>
  mutate(distance_from_pooled = abs(p_hat_green - pooled_green$p_hat)) |>
  arrange(distance_from_pooled) |>
  select(name, green, total, p_hat_green, distance_from_pooled)
```

We can find the pooled estimate for every color at once too:

```{r}
pooled_colors <- bags |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(blue, brown, green, orange, red, yellow),
    names_to = "color",
    values_to = "count"
  ) |>
  group_by(color) |>
  summarize(count = sum(count), total = sum(total)) |>
  mutate(p_hat = count / total)

pooled_colors

mm_colors <- c(
  blue = "#2f9fd7", brown = "#603a34", green = "#31ac55",
  orange = "#f26f22", red = "#b11224", yellow = "#fff200"
)

ggplot(pooled_colors, aes(x = p_hat, y = fct_reorder(color, p_hat), fill = color)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = mm_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Estimated proportion", y = NULL)
```

## Standard deviation vs. standard error

**Standard deviation**: how much do *individual M&Ms* vary? Each M&M is either green (1) or not green (0). For yes/no data like this, the standard deviation is $\sqrt{p (1 - p)}$. We don't know $p$, so we use our pooled estimate:

```{r}
sd_individual <- sqrt(pooled_green$p_hat * (1 - pooled_green$p_hat))
sd_individual
```

**Standard error**: how much do *sample proportions* vary from bag to bag? It's the standard deviation of the sampling distribution. We can measure it two ways:

1. Directly, by finding the standard deviation of everyone's $\widehat{p}$
2. With the formula, $\text{SE} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{p (1 - p)}{n}}$, where $n$ is the size of one bag

```{r}
# 1. Standard deviation of all the bags' p-hats
se_from_bags <- sd(bags$p_hat_green)
se_from_bags

# 2. Formula, using the average bag size
avg_bag_size <- mean(bags$total)
se_formula <- sd_individual / sqrt(avg_bag_size)
se_formula
```

They should be pretty close!

## Margins of error

### Your bag

If you only had your own bag, you could still estimate the standard error with the formula and find the margin of error: $\text{MOE} = 1.96 \times \text{SE}$. Then $\widehat{p} \pm \text{MOE}$ gives a range of plausible values for the true $p$ (a 95% confidence interval).

```{r}
my_bag <- bags |>
  filter(name == my_name) |>
  mutate(
    se = sqrt(p_hat_green * (1 - p_hat_green) / total),
    moe = 1.96 * se,
    lower = p_hat_green - moe,
    upper = p_hat_green + moe
  )

my_bag |> select(name, green, total, p_hat_green, se, moe, lower, upper)
```

That's pretty wide, since one bag only has about 50 M&Ms.

### The whole class

The pooled sample is much bigger, so the standard error and margin of error are much smaller:

```{r}
pooled_green <- pooled_green |>
  mutate(
    se = sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / total),
    moe = 1.96 * se,
    lower = p_hat - moe,
    upper = p_hat + moe
  )

pooled_green
```

Which one is more useful? Why?

## Do 95% of the intervals catch the truth?

In real life we never know the true $p$, so we can't check. But we *do* know it for the simulated bags, which were drawn from the Cleveland mix (`r scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(true_p_green)` green). Here's every simulated bag's 95% confidence interval. About 95% of them should include the true proportion (the dashed line):

```{r}
sim_cis <- sim_bags |>
  mutate(
    total = blue + brown + green + orange + red + yellow,
    p_hat_green = green / total,
    se = sqrt(p_hat_green * (1 - p_hat_green) / total),
    lower = p_hat_green - 1.96 * se,
    upper = p_hat_green + 1.96 * se,
    catches_truth = lower <= true_p_green & true_p_green <= upper
  )

ggplot(sim_cis, aes(x = p_hat_green, y = factor(bag), color = catches_truth)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_p_green, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(
    x = "Proportion of green M&Ms (with 95% confidence interval)",
    y = "Simulated bag",
    color = "Interval includes\nthe true p?"
  )

mean(sim_cis$catches_truth)
```

## What if we had way more bags?

The vat is a simulated population of 10,000 M&Ms, so we know its true proportion of green:

```{r}
vat_p_green <- mean(vat$color == "green")
vat_p_green
```

We can use `rep_slice_sample()` to pretend 1,000 students each got a bag of 50:

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
virtual_bags <- vat |>
  rep_slice_sample(n = 50, reps = 1000) |>
  summarize(p_hat_green = mean(color == "green"))

ggplot(virtual_bags, aes(x = p_hat_green)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, boundary = 0.01, color = "white", fill = "#31A84A") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = vat_p_green, linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of green M&Ms in each virtual bag", y = "Number of bags")

# The standard error from 1,000 virtual bags
sd(virtual_bags$p_hat_green)

# The standard error from the formula
sqrt(vat_p_green * (1 - vat_p_green) / 50)
```

That's a bell curve centered at the true proportion. That's the central limit theorem!
